summary: Describes the Diameter application used for authentication, authorization, and accounting in Network Access Server environments, used together with the Diameter base protocol and EAP. It was replaced by RFC 7155.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets a network login box check who you are, what you may do, and how much you used. A newer document replaced it.

subtitle: AAA (authentication, authorization, accounting) for network access servers using Diameter protocol.

tldr.problem: Network Access Servers (NAS) like dial-up gateways and wireless access points need to authenticate users, decide what they are authorized to do, and track their usage. Legacy RADIUS works for this, but has limitations in scalability and feature support.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4005 defines how the Diameter base protocol is used in NAS environments, specifying message types for authentication and authorization requests/answers, reauthentication, session termination, and accounting, while carefully maintaining compatibility with legacy RADIUS systems.
tldr.outcome: Provides a migration path from RADIUS to Diameter while maintaining backward compatibility. It was later updated by RFC 7155 with modernizations for contemporary network access scenarios.

today: RFC 4005 is a Standards Track specification that defined the foundational Diameter application for network access. It has been deployed in carrier networks worldwide and remains in use. RFC 7155 provides an updated version with enhancements for modern network requirements, and is recommended for new implementations. RFC 4005 continues to be valid and widely deployed.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
This RFC describes the Diameter protocol application used for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) services in the Network Access Server (NAS) environment. A NAS is any device that provides access service for users to a network, such as a dial-up access server, wireless access point, or broadband gateway. When a user connects to a NAS, the NAS needs to verify the user's identity, determine what services the user is allowed to use, and record usage for billing or auditing purposes.

The specification carefully designs interoperability with legacy RADIUS systems. Many initial Diameter deployments will include existing RADIUS infrastructure, so RFC 4005 includes the RADIUS attribute space in Diameter messages, minimizing the need for attribute translation at protocol conversion points. The interactions between Diameter and RADIUS specified in this document extend to all Diameter applications, not just NAS.
sections.plainLanguage: When you connect to the internet via a phone line, a cable modem, or WiFi, a network box checks if you have an account, what speed you can use, and counts how much data you transferred. This RFC describes how that conversation works.

sections.title: Session Lifecycle and Core Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines how AAA sessions are established, maintained, and terminated. When a user connects to a NAS, the NAS sends an AA-Request (AAR) message containing the user's identity and authentication information. The AAA server responds with an AA-Answer (AAA) message containing either authorization parameters or a failure code. For multi-round authentication (such as challenge-response protocols), the server can set a MULTI_ROUND_AUTH result code, causing the NAS to continue the exchange.

After successful authentication and authorization, the session is established. At any time, the server can initiate reauthentication via a Re-Auth-Request (RAR) message, which the NAS must answer with a Re-Auth-Answer (RAA). When the user disconnects or the service is terminated, the NAS sends a Session-Termination-Request (STR) to clean up server resources. The server can also force termination by sending an Abort-Session-Request (ASR). Accounting records track session usage via Accounting-Request (ACR) and Accounting-Answer (ACA) messages at session start, interim points, and termination.
sections.plainLanguage: The conversation goes: you ask 'can I log in?', the server checks and says yes or no. If yes, the server can later say 'log in again to make sure you're still you'. When you disconnect, you send 'I'm done' and the server forgets about you.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
The RFC defines AVPs (Attribute-Value Pairs) for various authentication methods used in NAS environments. These include User-Password (for PAP), CHAP authentication (Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol), and ARAP (AppleTalk Remote Access Protocol) credentials. The AA-Request message carries the user's identity and whichever authentication credential is appropriate for the connection type.

Authorization AVPs describe what the user is allowed to do. Service-Type indicates the category of service (login, framed access, etc.). Framed access AVPs specify network parameters like IP address, subnet mask, routing, IP compression, and MTU. Tunneling AVPs define tunnel parameters for VPN scenarios. Non-framed access AVPs specify login hosts and services. The response message may include callback numbers, idle timeouts, session timeouts, filter rules, and quality-of-service parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: You prove you're who you say you are (authentication). Once proven, the server tells you what you can do: use IPv4 or IPv6, which networks you can reach, how long you can stay idle before disconnect (authorization).

sections.title: Accounting and Usage Tracking
sections.content:
RFC 4005 defines the Accounting function, which tracks user sessions and resource usage for billing and auditing. When a session starts successfully, the NAS sends an Accounting-Request (ACR) with Accounting-Record-Type set to START_RECORD. During the session, the NAS can send interim accounting records (INTERIM_RECORD) containing cumulative usage statistics like input octets, output octets, input packets, and output packets.

When the session ends, a STOP_RECORD is sent containing final usage statistics. The server acknowledges each accounting request with an Accounting-Answer (ACA) containing the result code. Additional accounting AVPs include Acct-Session-Time (duration in seconds), Acct-Authentic (indicating the authentication method), Acct-Delay-Time, and tunnel-related accounting for sessions that use tunneling. This allows carriers and ISPs to bill users based on time, volume, or other metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a phone bill showing minutes used, accounting records show how many bytes you downloaded and for how long you were connected. The server stores these for your bill.

sections.title: RADIUS Compatibility and Interoperability
sections.content:
A significant feature of RFC 4005 is its careful design for backward compatibility with RADIUS. Diameter AVP codes 0-255 are reserved for RADIUS compatibility, mapping directly to RADIUS attribute codes. This allows existing RADIUS attributes to be used in Diameter without translation. The RFC defines interaction rules for gateways that must convert between RADIUS and Diameter protocols.

When a RADIUS Access-Request is forwarded as a Diameter AA-Request, most attributes map directly. When a Diameter AA-Request is forwarded to a RADIUS server, the RFC specifies which AVPs can be translated and which cannot. Some RADIUS attributes are prohibited in Diameter, and some Diameter AVPs are only for RADIUS compatibility. The RFC also addresses RADIUS Vendor-Specific Attributes (VSAs) and how they map to Diameter Vendor-Specific AVPs, enabling smooth migration of existing infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The old RADIUS system used specific tags for information. This RFC keeps those same tags so that old and new systems can talk to each other without confusion.

sections.title: Adoption and RFC 7155
sections.content:
RFC 4005 was published in August 2005 as a Standards Track specification. It defined the first complete Diameter application for network access and became widely deployed in carrier networks. The specification was based on requirements from RFC 2989 and RFC 3169, addressing both technical and operational needs of service providers.

As technology evolved and requirements changed, RFC 7155 was published in 2014 to provide an updated version of the NAS application with clarifications, additional AVPs for modern scenarios, and improved guidance for implementers. RFC 4005 remains valid and continues to be used in deployed systems, but RFC 7155 is recommended for new implementations that need support for contemporary authentication methods and network types.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC worked well for years and many companies used it. A newer version (RFC 7155) improved it for today's networks, but the original is still correct and still used.
